title: Everything we learned in 29 minutes at Harvard Business School (part 1)
summary: A crash course in the hard skills of an HBS MBA, taught through company examples: strategy (Porter's Five Forces and cost leadership vs. differentiation via Starbucks), marketing (STP via Warby Parker), product development (deep customer understanding and A/B testing via Netflix), and five finance concepts a CEO must understand to talk to a CFO and board. The sisters relate each framework to their own brand, Sisters Matcha.

ideas.idea: Strategy is a roadmap for where to compete and how to win; without a clear strategy even the best product or company will not succeed.
ideas.detail: Strategy is where HBS strives to differentiate itself; the hosts frame the episode as a mini Harvard MBA that saves you the $250,000 tuition (they spent $500,000 collectively on their two MBAs).

ideas.idea: Use Porter's Five Forces (threat of new entrants, supplier power, buyer power, threat of substitutes, rivalry) to understand any company's competitive landscape.
ideas.detail: Invented at HBS, it is the classic tool to ask of any company you evaluate. Applied to Starbucks: new-entrant threat is low because of brand, supply chain and real estate spend; supplier power is weak because Starbucks buys in huge volume (like Walmart and Costco); substitutes are moderate; rivalry is high but Starbucks wins on in-store experience and premium pricing.

ideas.idea: Companies reduce buyer bargaining power by building loyalty and switching costs, such as loyalty programs, seasonal drinks, and a prepaid app balance that acts as a ledger with the customer.
ideas.detail: Customers could go to Dunkin', Philz or Peet's, but Starbucks locks them in through the app and by owning the 'third space' idea, so 'let's meet at Starbucks' is ingrained from middle school on.

ideas.idea: Mitigate the threat of substitutes by expanding into adjacent categories rather than staying a single-channel retailer.
ideas.detail: Coffee has many substitutes (home, office), so Starbucks sells pods, beans and ground coffee to diversify beyond its retail stores.

ideas.idea: Getting ahead of bad press with a real apology and a customer-service focus is part of competing on experience.
ideas.detail: After an employee called the police on two Black men sitting in a Starbucks who had done nothing wrong, the company issued a forward apology and asked how to make it right; an HBR piece recently highlighted Starbucks going above and beyond on customer service.

ideas.idea: Porter's generic strategies say you must pick cost leadership or differentiation; you cannot be the cheapest, the best and the highest quality at the same time.
ideas.detail: Walmart ('everyday savings') is the cost leader and strips amenities to hit the lowest price; Starbucks chose differentiation with premium prices, third spaces, and high-touch operations like writing names and now personalized messages ('I love you so mucha') on cups.

ideas.idea: Sisters Matcha deliberately chose differentiation over cost leadership because its supplier cost, rarity and the founders' personal brand made a premium positioning the only coherent choice.
ideas.detail: Their matcha uses the Okumidori cultivar, which is only 2% of matcha produced in Japan, hand-picked, ceremonial grade and first harvest; a cost-leadership brand would not align with something you put in your body daily for health.

ideas.idea: STP (segmenting, targeting, positioning) is the backbone of any marketing campaign or go-to-market: identify customer groups, choose one, craft a message for it and make it stick.
ideas.detail: Warby Parker segmented eyewear buyers into high-end brand seekers (Prada, Gucci), the cost-conscious, and millennials wanting trendy but affordable, then targeted the third group.

ideas.idea: If you try to serve everyone you serve no one: pick one target segment and build the whole brand around their hopes, frustrations and values.
ideas.detail: Warby Parker built for online-first millennials with $95-100 pricing and a buy-a-pair-give-a-pair program, positioned as modern, chic, accessible, digital-first and socially conscious; it disrupted Luxottica, which controlled 80-90% of eyewear (including Ray-Ban) when cute glasses cost $300+, and is now valued at over $1 billion. The best products the hosts have used are hyper-focused on understanding their customers deeply.

ideas.idea: Conscious consumerism was a novel differentiator 10-15 years ago (TOMS, Warby Parker) that created brand loyalists, and it is now taken for granted as part of many companies' DNA.
ideas.detail: TOMS gave a pair of shoes to a child in a developing country for every pair bought; later brands like Rothy's (recycled water bottle shoes) and Blueland built on the sustainability bend.

ideas.idea: In product development you cannot guess at a customer's problem; identify it very specifically, iterate like crazy, test everything, and pivot when new data arrives.
ideas.detail: Between them the sisters have almost 20 years in product. Netflix is the case: it famously A/B tests every detail, including per-user thumbnails, so Jean sees Henry Golding in a thumbnail even when he is a secondary character because Netflix learned she is likelier to click.

ideas.idea: HBS's goal for finance is not to make every graduate a modeling genius but to make CEOs who can understand the CFO and the board and make decisions with confidence.
ideas.detail: The CEO's job is not to be the expert; the CFO is the right-hand expert who helps make decisions with the information. Cherie prefers adjusting projections with finance counterparts over building models herself.

ideas.idea: Revenue is money coming through the door; profit is what is left after bills are paid, and billions in revenue can still be unprofitable if costs are high.
ideas.detail: For Netflix, revenue is subscription fees and profit is what remains after servers, employees and content costs.

ideas.idea: Cash flow is the item closest to your bank account and differs from profit because upfront investments can sit on the balance sheet as assets while the cash is gone.
ideas.detail: Netflix spends billions upfront producing shows that are booked as assets. Some businesses are cash poor while boring businesses can throw off recurring cash.

ideas.idea: Unit economics, the margin per unit or per customer, always comes up when evaluating a company, and customer acquisition cost must make sense against lifetime value.
ideas.detail: If a Netflix subscription brings in $10 but content costs $12 per subscriber, the company loses money; Netflix's data scientists spend a lot of time on this. For Sisters Matcha the unit is a single can: cost to make and ship one can to a first-time customer.

ideas.idea: Runway is how long your money lasts at the current burn rate, and a CEO must always watch it to stay afloat.
ideas.detail: Spending $100,000 a year with $200,000 in the bank means two years of runway.

ideas.idea: Valuation metrics like P/E and EV/EBITDA are just how investors express a company's worth, and the number means nothing outside the context of its category.
ideas.topic: Finance industry: VC, PE, banking, hedge funds
ideas.detail: A price-to-earnings ratio of 20 can mean a company is doing amazingly or is below the bar depending on whether it is tech or industrials; do not be afraid of the acronyms.
